title: Cu nanoparticles deposited on CNT by supercritical fluid deposition for electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: Climate change has turned into one of the most important concerns for scientist in the last years due to the huge increase of CO2 concentration in the atmosphere in the last century. Electrocatalytic reduction seems to be a very promising technology to help to reduce industrial CO2 emissions. The development of catalysts capable of activating the CO2 molecule is the main challenge of this technology. In this work a copper supported on carbon nanotubes (Cu/CNT) catalyst has been synthesized using supercritical fluid deposition (SFD) and assembled into a polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) type cell to carry out the electrochemical reduction of CO2. The influence of current density, temperature and CO2 flowrate has been analysed and results have been compared with those previously obtained with Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts synthesized by SFD. The CO2 reduction rate and the products distribution attained with the three catalysts have been analysed. CO has been the main reaction product attained with the Cu/CNT catalyst developed in this work, followed by small amounts of formic acid and methane. This can be considered the main difference observed in relation with Pt or Pb based catalysts that promote the production of formic acid as main reaction product. This can be considered the main difference observed in relation with Pt or Pb based catalysts that promote the production of formic acid as main reaction product. 1. Introduction Carbon dioxide emissions have been considered as one of the most important concerns of our society in terms of environmental impact in the last years. Climate experts advise that CO2 emissions must be drastically reduced in the next decades to keep safe our planet. Nevertheless, it is a difficult challenge since the prediction of different energy administrations point out that fossil fuels will continue to be the main sources of energy in the next years. Among the actions that can have a significant impact on CO2 emissions lessening are the Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU) technologies. Among CCU practices, the conversion of CO2 to fuels could have a significant impact by reusing a huge amount of CO2 [1]. For that purpose, the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 is a promising technology, since it can achieve high conversion rates compared to other technologies, such as the photocatalytic processes [2] and can be used to exploit
3
excess electricity (from renewable intermittent sources) to produce fuels. This approach is known as “power to fuels” [3] and has received increasing attention due to the need of storing energy subjected to intermittent production (and difficult forecast). Regarding the electrochemical reduction of CO2, the development of efficient, selective and stable catalysts represents the greatest challenge for the implementation of this technology on an industrial scale [4]. Likewise, the operating conditions in the electrochemical cell are important, and it is expected that the current studies will probably allow to achieve, within a medium or long-term horizon, a reasonable electrocatalytic performance in terms of cell voltage, current density, and faradaic efficiency [5]. Many works have focus on the search of electrocatalysts, usually based on metals or metal oxides, with the capacity to convert CO2 to valuable compounds. In this sense, Hori and collaborators [6,7] reported an exhaustive classification of metals based on their activity towards the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in an aqueous electrolyte. These works highlighted the activity of Cu towards the formation of hydrocarbons (methane and ethylene), the capacity of Pb, Hg, In, Sn and Tl to promote the production of formic acid, as well as the activity of Au, Ag, Zn, Pb and Ga towards the formation of CO. Other subsequent work has studied the behaviour of different transition metal foils (Au, Ag, Zn, Cu, Ni, Pt, and Fe) in the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to methane and methanol [8] in aqueous electrolyte. They reported that all these metals are capable of producing methane or methanol (at low rate for most of them), and that the activity of these metals towards CO2 electrochemical reduction follow this order: Au, Ag, Zn > Cu > Ni, Pt, Fe, what was attributed to their CO binding energy. Despite these thorough classifications, the approach of using gas diffusion electrodes (GDE) instead of metal foils or meshes as electrodes has opened the range of
4
possibilities. Gas diffusion electrodes usually involve an electrocatalyst dispersed on a gas diffusion layer. The development of electrocatalysts based on nanostructures (of different morphology, crystallinity, specific surface) in the reduction of CO2 has motivated the study of metal nanoparticles on different carbon supports. In this context, the group of Professor Valverde synthesized electrocatalysts comprised of Cu nanoparticles on activated carbon and on carbon nanofibres for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in gas phase [9]. For its part, the group of Professor Centi has studied the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in gas phase in a PEM (polymer electrolyte membrane) type cell using Pt and Fe on carbon nanotubes (CNT) [10] and Fe, Fe-Co and Cu on CNT doped with nitrogen (N-CNT) [11]. They have also studied Cu nanoparticles on CNT [12] and Fe on carbon doped with N [13]. On the other hand, Wang et. al [14] studied the use of commercial Pt/C and Pd/C and synthesized Cu/CNT as electrocatalysts in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in gas phase. These authors used fuel cell type reactors based on alkaline anion-exchange membrane and proton exchange membrane (AAEM and PEM, respectively). All these works point out that the use of nanostructured catalysts deposited on carbon supports result in the reduction of CO2 into valuable products. Nevertheless, CO2 conversion rates and selectivity values still have ample leeway for improvement. Carbon nanotubes have been used as support of electrocatalysts in some works, as stated before [10–12,14]. The interesting results obtained, when comparing with other supports, have been attributed to the promotion of surface transport of protons, which facilitates the obtention of products (such as alcohols) of longer chain [11]. Numerous works in the literature study the use of copper as catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 from the experimental and the modelling points of view [15,16]. Nevertheless, there are few works approaching the use of copper
5
nanoparticles deposited on carbon nanotubes integrating GDE in gas phase cells, and this is precisely what we propose in this work. On the other hand, it is well known that the synthesis method used to obtain catalysts comprised of nanoparticles influence notably on their characteristics [17,18]. In this context, a very interesting synthesis method for the deposition of metallic nanoparticles in porous supports is the supercritical fluid deposition (SFD). This technique presents a series of advantages compared to other synthesis methods. Since the mass transport properties of supercritical fluids are similar to those of gases (diffusion coefficient, surface tension…) they can easily penetrate the pores of porous supports (contrary to what happens with methods that imply the use of liquids to dissolve the metal precursor). Likewise, high concentrations of metal precursor are achieved on the surface of the support, due to the solvent power of supercritical fluids, which is similar to that of liquids. This facilitates the faster deposition of nanoparticles compared to chemical vapour deposition, CVD, the most commonly used method at industrial scale [19]. The synthesis of electrocatalysts with copper nanoparticles deposited on carbon nanotubes (Cu/CNT) has been addressed in this work. The activity of Cu/CNT in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 in gas phase has been studied in a PEM type cell. As far as we know, a Cu/CNT electrocatalyst synthesized by supercritical fluid deposition has not been used for the electroreduction of CO2. On the other hand, Higgins et al. [20] pointed out the huge opportunity to investigate the influence of different parameters to move forward the design of practical electrolysers involving GDE for CO2 electroreduction in gas phase. In this regard, the influence of current density (within 8 - 24 mA cm-2), temperature (40 - 80 ºC) and CO2 flowrate (0.02 - 0.08 SL min -1) has been studied in terms of CO2 conversion rate and selectivity. In addition, the results attained with Cu/CNT have been compared with those previously reported using Pt/CNT and
6
Pb/CNT catalysts (synthesized by supercritical fluid deposition) in the same PEM type cell.

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Synthesis of Cu/CNT catalyst using supercritical CO2
sections.text: The experimental set-up used for the deposition of metal nanoparticles onto carbon nanotubes has been previously described in several works [21–23]. It includes an ad-hoc 100 ml stainless steel reactor supplied by DEMEDE Engineering and Research with a temperature controller (TOHO, TTM-204) and a high pressure pump (P-50, Thar SFC, supplied by Productos de Instrumentación, S.A., Spain) to increase CO2 pressure.

sections.heading: 2.1.2. CO2 electroreduction
sections.text:
The experimental set-up used for the electroreduction of carbon dioxide has been described in previous works [21–23]. It includes a PEM (Proton Echange Membrane) type electrochemical cell (single cell PaxiTech supplied by MICROBEAM, electrode area: 25 cm2). Cu/CNT catalyst is coated in carbon paper and assembled by hot pressing to a Nafion® proton exchange membrane that separates anodic and cathodic compartments. The set-up includes a peristaltic pump (DINKO- D21-V) that circulates a KHCO3 solution into the anodic part of the cell, a temperature controller that allows fixing the temperature and a mass flow controller (BROOKS, F27497 – 001) that allows modifying the CO2 flowrate in the cathodic part of the cell. Current is fixed with a potentiostat-galvanostat ((PGSTAT302N, Metrohm AUTOLAB) that also measures voltage and allows performing linear sweep voltammetries (LSV). 2.2. Analytical methods 2.2.1. Characterization of Cu/CNT catalysts
7
Different techniques have been used to characterize the Cu/CNT catalyst synthesised using supercritical fluid deposition:
• TEM (Transmission Electron Microscopy) has been measured in a Jeol 2100
TEM microscope operating at 200 kV equipped with a side entry double-tilt (±25°) sample holder and EDS detector (Oxford Link) in an external lab (Instituto de Energías Renovables, Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha). The size distribution of metal nanoparticles deposited onto the carbon nanotubes from the TEM micrographs using DigitalMicrograph software (supplied by Gatan Software Team) was also analysed in that external lab. • ICP-AES (Inductively Coupled Plasma, Atomic Emission Spectrometry) has
been analysed in an ICP-AES Liberty Sequential (VARIAN)) to analyse the copper concentration deposited onto the carbon nanotubes. • XRD (X-ray diffraction) has been determined in an XRD Philips, X́Pert MPD
to determine the copper species deposited onto the carbon nanotubes.
• Linear sweep voltammetries have been made to analyse the electrochemical
behaviour of the catalysts. These voltammetries were developed in the PEM type electrochemical cell just before each experiment once the experimental conditions have been achieved. The scan was made between 0 and 4 V with a scan rate of 0.1 V s-1 and a step of 0.02 V. It must be noted that voltammetries have been done in the electrochemical cell, which does not have a reference electrode. That means that the voltage applied is the cell voltage (between the working electrode and the counter electrode) instead of the working electrode voltage versus a reference electrode that is usually employed in aqueous electrolyte cells [24].
2.2.2. CO2 electroreduction products
8
The analytical method used to determine the reaction products formed during the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide has been described in previous works [21,23]. Gas products have been analysed using a gas chromatograph (GC 7890A supplied by Agilent) equipped with FID and TCD detectors that includes a solid phase microextraction (SPME) fibre (GC Sampler 80) used to analyse the liquid products obtained.

sections.heading: 2.3.1. Synthesis of Cu/CNT catalyst using supercritical CO2
sections.text: The experimental procedure for the synthesis of Cu/CNT catalyst using supercritical fluid deposition technique has been described in previous works [21,23]. 0.25 g of carbon nanotubes and 0.25 g of metal precursor (copper acetylacetonate) are loaded into the reactor. Then, the reactor is connected to the experimental setup, purged with CO2 (at cylinder pressure ~60 bar) and heated up. Once the reactor reaches the set-point temperature (200 ºC) the pressure of CO2 is increased by pumping up to 100 bar and maintained at these conditions (in batch mode) for 60 minutes to achieve the dissolution of the metal precursor. Then, hydrogen is introduced inside the reactor and pressure is increased up to 250 bar for 30 minutes to reduce the metal precursor to its metallic form. Finally, and once the reactor is depressurized, the product obtained is vacuum filtered (0.45 µm Nylon) and the catalyst obtained is then dried in an oven at 40 ºC during 24 hours.

sections.heading: 2.3.2. CO2 electroreduction
sections.text:
The experimental procedure carried out for the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide has been described in previous works [21,23]. The catalysts obtained from the supercritical fluid deposition have been used to prepare a catalytic ink. This ink is then sprayed on two pieces of carbon paper (Toray® Teflon TM treated) using an airbrush to
9
form the catalytic layer of the GDE. A metal load of 0.4 mg of metal cm-2 has been deposited for each electrode. Both pieces of carbon paper are then assembled to both sides of a Nafion® 117 membrane (in contact with the catalytic layer) by hot pressing. This assembly is set in the PEM type cell. To carry out the electroreduction experiments, a KHCO3 solution is circulated through the anodic part of the electrochemical cell while a continuous CO2 flowrate is passed on the cathodic flow channel of the cell. The experiments are made under galvanostatic operation mode for two hours. Gas products obtained are circulated to the GC while liquids are collected in a cold trap for further analysis by SPME in the GC. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Characterization of Cu/CNT catalysts synthesized Transmission electronic microscopy, X-ray diffraction and ICP have been used to characterize the Cu/CNT catalyst developed in this work. Figure 1 shows two of the micrographs taken using TEM as well as the nanoparticle size distribution obtained from the micrographs. As it can be appreciated in figure 1a, copper nanoparticles (black dots in the image) seem to be homogenously dispersed onto the carbon nanotubes surface. In addition, Figure 1b shows that the size of the nanoparticles formed can be small enough to be deposited inside the carbon nanotubes (inner diameter of 4.5 nm ± 0.5 nm according to the supplier). The size distribution of
the copper nanoparticles confirms these observations. As it can be seen in figure 1c most of the particles have a mean diameter between 1.5 and 5 nm showing a normal distribution with most of the particles with diameters around 2 and 3 nm. Furthermore, around 14 % of the nanoparticles have a mean diameter above 6 nm, in some cases due to the agglomeration of nanoparticles.
10
Figure 2 shows the XRD pattern for the Cu/CNT catalyst synthesised through supercritical deposition technique. The diffraction lines at 2θ = 43.2, 50.5 and 74.2º can be clearly defined and correspond to the characteristic (111), (200) and (220) planes of the faced-centered cubic (fcc) crystal lattice of metallic copper (Standard diffraction angle JCDPS Copper 04-0836: 2θ = 43.297, 50.433, 74.130º). This demonstrate that the supercritical fluid deposition method can successfully deposit metallic copper onto the surface of carbon nanotubes. Some peaks associated to copper oxide (Cu2O) are also appreciated probably because samples were not preserved in inert atmosphere.
From the XRD pattern obtained the mean diameter of copper nanoparticles has been determined using the Scherrer´s equation (equation 1) [25,26] for the line 2θ = 43.2º. The crystallite size of the copper nanoparticles has been 4.3 nm, what is in accordance with the most frequent values calculated from the size distribution attained from TEM micrographs.

ICP has been used to determine the copper concentration in the catalyst. A 16.6 % of copper was deposited onto the carbon nanotubes. Taking into account that initially a 19.5 % of copper was added with the carbon nanotubes, it means that the copper deposition yield using the supercritical deposition method was of 85.1 %.
From the results obtained during the characterization of the Cu/CNT catalyst synthesised using supercritical fluid deposition method, it can be concluded that metallic copper is successfully deposited onto the surface of the carbon nanotubes (some of them inside the nanotubes according to TEM micrographs) with a deposition
11
efficiency higher than 80 %. Furthermore, TEM analysis shows a homogeneous particle distribution with a mean diameter between 2 and 5 nm.

sections.heading: 3.2. CO2 electroreduction
sections.text:
The Cu/CNT catalyst synthesized using supercritical fluid deposition has been used to carry out the electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide in a PEM type electrochemical cell. The influence of different parameters such as current density, temperature and CO2 flowrate in the distribution of products as well as in the CO2 reduction yield has been analysed. Furthermore, results obtained with Cu/CNT as catalyst have been compared with those obtained in previous works using Pt/CNT [21] and Pb/CNT [23] to try to identify the main differences between the use of different nanostructured metals as catalytic material. Just before each CO2 electroreduction assay, linear sweep voltammetries (LSV) have been performed in the PEM type cell to characterize the electrochemical behaviour of the electrode assembly in the cell. In this sense, Figure 4 shows the LSV with Cu/CNT catalyst for different values of temperature and CO2 flowrate. As it can be observed, for cell voltages above 2.5 V higher values of current density are obtained at 60 ºC than at 40 ºC, which indicates a higher activity of the Cu/CNT catalyst in reduction reactions at 60 ºC. When analysing CO2 flowrate a higher current density is observed (and then a higher electrochemical activity of the catalyst) at higher flowrate (0.05 L min-1) especially for cell voltages above 2.5 V. According to these results, higher CO2 conversion rates are expected working at 60 ºC than at 40 ºC and at 0.05 L CO2 min -1 than at 0.02 L CO2 min -1. Nevertheless, the H2O reduction reaction (Hydrogen Evolution Reaction, HER) inevitably competes with that of CO2 reduction in the cathode. Voltamperometric data
12
cannot be used to distinguish the amount of current due to each of these competing reactions. For this reason, the operation conditions which would lead to higher CO2 conversion rates cannot be certainly indicated without the analysis of the reaction products formed in the cathodic compartment. In this context, Figure 4 shows the product formation rate obtained using the Cu/CNT catalyst synthesized through supercritical fluid deposition technique as a function of current density, temperature and CO2 flowrate. It can be observed that the main product formed is CO, followed by small amounts of formic acid (whose production rate is less than half than that of CO in most cases) and methane in a lesser extent. In addition, very low amounts of other products such as methanol or acetone have also been detected (an enlargement of figure 4 is shown in Figure S1 in the supporting information to better appreciate the formation of minority products such as methanol and acetone). CO production rate increases with current density but specially with temperature and CO2 flowrate. The rest of products barely change with those parameters. According to several authors [6–8,27] copper seems to be the unique metal that allows the formation of hydrocarbons (such as methane or ethylene) and alcohols at considerable reaction rates. Nevertheless, in this work it has been observed that in the experimental conditions analysed copper catalyst (Cu/CNT) favours the conversion of CO2 to CO instead of the formation of hydrocarbons. This behaviour could be attributed to the very low size of the copper nanoparticles produced with the supercritical fluids deposition technique (between 2 and 5 nm). In this sense, many works have determined the influence of the copper nanoparticles size in the product distribution from CO2 reduction [24,28,29]. From all of these works, the results obtained by Reske et al. [24] are especially interesting as they compared the activity of copper nanoparticles with sizes between 2 and 15 nm with the activity of a copper foil. In that work, they
13
determined that the use of copper nanoparticles within the interval studied promoted the conversion of CO2 to CO instead of methane, as it is observed in this work with the Cu/CNT catalyst studied. In this context, there are other works in literature that use copper nanoparticles as catalytic material in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 that also obtained CO as main reduction product. Is the case of Wang et al. [14] that observed the formation of CO, or Merino-García et al. [28] that observed the formation of CO followed by methane. In this context, it has to be pointed that most of the works that inform about the formation of methane or ethylene as main reaction products during the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide have been developed with the CO2 dissolved in an aqueous electrolyte. On the other hand, those works carried out in gas phase obtained carbon monoxide as main product during the reduction of CO2 [14,30]. Results obtained with Cu/CNT have been compared with those previously obtained with Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts in the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide [21,23]. In this sense, Figure 5 shows the LSV obtained when using copper as catalyst compared with those obtained with platinum and lead, to try to determine the main differences between those three metals supported onto CNT used as catalysts. As it can be appreciated, a very similar behaviour is obtained with the three metals compared, although copper seems to achieve a slightly higher current density for cell voltages above 3.3 V. The distribution of products (selectivity) obtained during the electroreduction of CO2 can be considered the main difference between the use of Cu/CNT, Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts. Thus, Figure 6 compares the products distribution attained with those three catalysts at the same experimental conditions. It can be observed that Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts promote mainly the production of formic acid with low amounts of
14
CO and methane. The main differences between platinum and lead are the higher proportion of methane obtained with Pt/CNT and the higher one of methanol with Pb/CNT as determined in previous works [21,23]. On the contrary, copper does not tend to produce formic acid but CO as main product. It must be noted that the production rate of formic acid is very similar with the three electrocatalysts being the main difference the much higher CO production obtained with Cu/CNT. There are many works in literature [31,32] that try to explain the reaction mechanisms for CO2 electroreduction. A simplified reaction scheme generally accepted is shown in Figure S2 in the supporting information. That scheme is based in the reaction mechanisms proposed in different works [6,8,27,33]. Hence, the first step is the activation of the CO2 molecule, which needs a high overpotential due to the stability of CO2. Nevertheless, this overpotential can be reduced by the use of an appropriate electrocatalyst, that favours the adsorption of the CO2 molecule onto the catalyst to form the CO2 * ads radical. Then, this radical can react through two different pathways. First, it can be protonated to be converted into the CO2H * ads radical, that can be desorbed to form the formiate anion (HCOO -) in aqueous media (pathway A in figure S2). The second reaction pathway (pathway B in the scheme) involves the reduction of the CO2 * radical to CO*ads, which can be then desorbed to form CO or it can remain adsorbed and be further reduced to form products such as methanol, methane and other products with one or more carbons. Thus, and attending to this reaction scheme, it is not strange that formic acid and CO are the main reaction products during the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide [14,34–36]. As previously said Hori and co-workers [6,7] determined that several metals favour the reaction pathway A (such as Sn, Ti, Cd or Pb) and some other favour the reaction
15
pathway B (i.e. Ga, Zn, Ag, Au or Cu). From the second group, copper seems to be the unique that allows the formation of hydrocarbons (methane or ethylene) and alcohols at considerable reaction rates, according to several authors [8,27]. The percentage of products corresponding to pathway B (related to the total CO2 products formed) has been calculated for each experimental condition tested with the three catalysts compared. These values are shown in Table 1. It can be observed that when using Cu/CNT catalyst the products formed through pathway B are in most cases higher than 80 % whereas for Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts are less than 30 %. These results indicate that Cu/CNT favours reaction pathway B whereas Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT promote reaction pathway A in most of the experimental conditions studied. However, some exceptions have been observed, such as the behaviour of Pb/CNT when working at 80 ºC. In that conditions formic acid is barely produced whereas methanol and CO are promoted.

Figure 7 shows the CO2 reduction rate for the three catalysts compared in this work. As it can be observed, the evolution of the CO2 conversion rate with the different parameters studied is different depending on the catalyst used. First of all, it can be appreciated that, in every case, CO2 conversion rate is higher when using Cu/CNT catalyst. As it can be seen in Figure 7a CO2 conversion rate increases linearly with current density with Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts. On the contrary, it shows a
16
maximum at current density 16 mA cm-2 with the Cu/CNT catalyst. The decrease of CO2 conversion rate observed between 16 and 24 mA cm -2 could be due to mass transfer limitations close to the catalyst nanoparticles (in the GDE) when increasing current density applied, together with other phenomena that could cause a change in the selectivity of the catalyst from CO to formic acid (pathway B to pathway A in the scheme of Figure S2). The results obtained with Cu/CNT catalyst are in accordance with those reported in literature by Merino-García et al., 2018 [28] which observed an increase of CO2 conversion rate when increasing current density up to a certain current density value (15 mA cm-2) and from that point conversion rate decreased.
As it is shown in Figure 7b CO2 conversion rate increases with temperature with
Cu/CNT catalyst. This could be attributed to an increase in the catalytic activity of the Cu/CNT catalyst (according to Arrhenius Law). As well an increase in the temperature inside the cell cause a higher agitation state of the electrons and then, a higher electrical conductivity what is traduced in a lower cell voltage (as it can be seen in Figure S3 in supporting information) which should favour CO2 reactions against water reduction. Nevertheless, this increase seems to be higher when temperature increases from 40 to 60 ºC than when it increases from 60 to 80 ºC. This can be caused by a decrease in the conductivity of Nafion® membrane for values close to 90 ºC [37]. In the case of Pt/CNT catalyst CO2 conversion rate keeps constant independently of the temperature applied in the interval studied. On the other side, Pb/CNT catalyst leads to a maximum value of CO2 conversion at 60 ºC and then it considerably decreases at 80 ºC. These results indicate an important reduction in the catalytic activity of the Pb/CNT catalyst at 80 ºC to generate formic acid related to that for CO, which is traduced in a decrease in the global CO2 reduction rate. Likewise, a lower conductivity of the membrane could contribute to that lower CO2 conversion rate at high temperature [37].

It can be observed that results obtained with the three catalysts are very similar when working at high current density and at low temperature and CO2 flowrate. In the rest of experimental conditions studied, Cu/CNT allows achieving a much higher conversion rate than Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT catalysts (between 5 and 27 times higher depending on the metal and the experimental conditions). The higher CO2 conversion rates attained with Cu/CNT catalyst could be attributed to the good properties of Cu for CO2 electroreduction [6,8] as well as the increase of CO2 conversion activity observed for small copper nanoparticles (< 5 nm) reported by Reske et al. [24]. The maximum CO2 conversion rate obtained in this work has been 0.151 mmol CO2 h -1 (when working at 16 mA cm-2, 60 ºC and 0.08 SL CO2 min -1) with Cu/CNT. The comparison of this conversion rate with those reported in the literature shows the good behaviour of Cu/CNT synthesized by supercritical fluid deposition in this work. This conversion rate is between one and two orders of magnitude higher than those reported by the group of Professor Valverde that studied the use of different electrocatalysts based on Cu nanoparticles (30 - 96 nm) [9,38]. On the other hand, the group of Professor Irabien studied the use of commercial Cu nanoparticles (60 - 80 nm) for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 [30], achieving practically the same maximum value of conversion rate that the one reported in this work. Regarding the use of Cu/CNT by other authors, Wang et al. [14] used this catalyst in two cell type reactors: an alkaline anion-exchange membrane and a proton exchange membrane type (AAEM and PEM, respectively). They found a 70 % lesser value for the maximum CO2 conversion rate with their AAEM cell than the one presented in this work. However, they did not observe CO2 conversion with their PEM cell (despite of using Cu/CNT catalyst). These results indicate the important influence of the cell design and the operating conditions on the CO2 electroreduction rate.
19
From the results obtained in this work it can be affirmed that the use of copper as catalyst seems to obtain much better results in the conversion of carbon dioxide than those previously obtained with platinum and lead based catalysts with a huge increase in the formation of CO as main product. Nevertheless, it must be pointed that the current efficiency values achieved with the electrochemical cell used in this work are still far away from those needed for a practical application. Current efficiencies obtained with the three catalysts compared in this work are shown in Figure S4 of the supporting information. According to that figure, current efficiency is below 3 % in every case, but it must be noted that Cu/CNT catalyst achieves efficiencies up to 5 times higher than Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT specially when working at low current density, high temperature and high CO2 flowrate. 4. Conclusions The main conclusions attained in this work are:
• Supercritical fluid deposition (SFD) technique attained a homogeneous
deposition of copper nanoparticles on carbon nanotubes surface with an efficiency higher than 85 % and a most frequent particle size between 2 and 5 nm. • Cu/CNT catalyst synthesized through SFD technique allows converting CO2 to
CO as main reaction product followed by small amounts of formic acid and methane. • CO production increases with temperature and CO2 flowrate. The maximum
CO2 conversion rate obtained has been 0.15 mmol h -1. This value is similar and, in some cases, higher than those reported in literature with Cu based electrocatalysts.
20
• When comparing the results obtained with Cu/CNT catalysts with those
previously obtained with Pt/CNT and Pb/CNT it can be observed that the main difference is related to the products distribution. Thus, copper leads to the production of CO as main product from CO2 reduction while platinum and lead tend to form mainly formic acid. • CO2 conversion rate is higher with the Cu/CNT catalyst than with Pt/CNT or
Pb/CNT especially at high values of temperature and CO2 flowrate and at low values of current density. At these experimental conditions, it is around 8 - 9 times higher with Cu/CNT.
